OUR SCIENCE

Playful by design.
Inspired by research.

Can digital practice help autistic children build everyday skills? Published studies offer encouraging findings in specific areas. Here is a family-friendly look at the evidence.

Social connectionEmotional skillsLanguage learning

What the research tells us.

Digital interventions are not all the same. Tablet activities, wearable tools and immersive VR have different designs and evidence. The studies below evaluated other systems, not LumiBrain™. They help explain the approach; they do not establish LumiBrain™'s effectiveness.

01
IMMERSIVE VR · CONTROLLED STUDY · 2018

Practising emotional and social skills.

A Hong Kong VR programme used six everyday scenarios. The accompanying report describes 94 children completing the study and 72 included in analysis. The training group improved in emotional expression/regulation and social interaction/adaptation; group-by-time differences were reported for affective expression and social reciprocity.

Why it matters: virtual scenarios can offer structured opportunities to rehearse social-emotional skills.

Keep in mind: this used an immersive room-based system, not LumiBrain™'s headset. The evidence concerns specific measured skills and should not be read as improvement in every autism-related symptom.

Read the study ↗

Yuan & Ip. Using virtual reality to train emotional and social skills in children with autism spectrum disorder. Developmental Neurorehabilitation, 2018. DOI: 10.1080/17571472.2018.1483000. Related programme report: Ip et al., Computers & Education, 2018; 10.1016/j.compedu.2017.09.010. These reports concern the same programme and are not separate independent trials.

02
VIRTUAL SOCIAL PRACTICE · PILOT STUDY · 2016

A space to explore social situations.

Thirty autistic children aged 7–16 completed ten one-hour virtual social-cognition sessions over five weeks. Before-and-after testing found gains in emotion recognition, social attribution and analogical reasoning.

Why it matters: engaging virtual practice may support selected social-cognitive skills.

Keep in mind: this was a small pre–post study without a randomised comparison group. It used a desktop virtual-world approach; it does not establish the effect of a home VR headset or long-term everyday benefits.

Read the study ↗

Didehbani et al. Virtual Reality Social Cognition Training for children with high functioning autism. Computers in Human Behavior, 2016;62:703–711. DOI: 10.1016/j.chb.2016.04.033.

03
WEARABLE DIGITAL SUPPORT · RANDOMISED TRIAL · 2019

Learning social cues at home.

A randomised trial enrolled 71 autistic children aged 6–12. Superpower Glass, an emotion-cue wearable, was added to existing behavioural support and compared with behavioural support alone. The study reported a significant benefit on the Vineland socialisation measure.

Why it matters: a digital tool can be studied as an addition to existing family and professional support.

Keep in mind: benefits were not significant across all four primary measures. Smart glasses are not immersive VR, and the findings are specific to this intervention used alongside existing support.

Read the study ↗

Voss et al. Effect of Wearable Digital Intervention for Improving Socialization in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Pediatrics, 2019;173:446–454. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2019.0285.

04
TABLET-BASED LEARNING · OBSERVATIONAL STUDY · 2020

Digital exercises and language development.

A three-year observational MITA study included 6,454 autistic children aged 2–12. Highly engaged users were compared with matched participants. The authors reported greater gains in receptive and expressive language scores, but no statistically significant differences on other untargeted subscales.

Why it matters: structured digital activities are being investigated for specific developmental goals.

Keep in mind: this was not a randomised trial. Parent-reported outcomes, engagement-based group selection and developer involvement limit causal conclusions. MITA is a tablet application, not VR or LumiBrain™.

Read the study ↗

Vyshedskiy et al. Novel Prefrontal Synthesis Intervention Improves Language in Children with Autism. Healthcare, 2020;8:566. DOI: 10.3390/healthcare8040566.

RESEARCH, IN PERSPECTIVE

Encouraging possibilities.
Individual journeys.

These studies suggest potential benefits in selected language, social and emotional skills. They do not prove a cure, improvement in all symptoms, or the effectiveness of LumiBrain™. Larger, independent studies and long-term follow-up remain important.
